frase_gancho.texto: Frida wore twenty-eight corsets between nineteen forty and nineteen fifty-four, and she painted several of them.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue to the next display case in Frida’s wardrobe.

guion_corto.texto: These corsets are not clothing. They are medical devices. Frida wore them to support a spine that had been damaged since the accident of nineteen twenty-five. Between nineteen forty and nineteen fifty-four she had to wear twenty-eight of them. But she did not simply hide them. Some she painted with religious and political symbols. One of the best known bears the hammer and sickle, along with other drawings. Look for those paintings on the plaster. Instead of hiding the device, she turned it into a canvas. Later she painted a steel corset in her painting La columna rota, from nineteen forty-four. Look closely at the plaster and the straps.

guion_largo.texto:
This display case shows Frida’s orthopedic corsets. They look like hard, cold objects, and they are. But they also have paint, drawings, and symbols. They are one of the places where her medical life and her life as an artist meet.

It all began with the accident of September seventeenth, nineteen twenty-five. Frida fractured her spine in three places and had to wear a plaster corset. Throughout her life, her spine caused her pain and complications. It is estimated that between nineteen forty and nineteen fifty-four she wore twenty-eight different corsets and went through several back operations.

The corsets were made of different materials. There were plaster ones, leather ones, and steel ones. The plaster ones were molded onto the body and left to dry. They were heavy and rigid, and wearing one meant moving the body with great difficulty.

Frida painted them. Some of them have drawings with religious and communist symbols. The best known bears a hammer and sickle, and other figures painted on the plaster. In those years, she believed that communism could relieve the suffering of the sick and the poor. Painting her corset with those ideas was a way of declaring which side she was on, even when she had to lie in bed.

That decision changes the way we look at the object. A medical corset is normally hidden under clothing. Frida made hers visible. She decorated it the way she decorated her clothes, her house, and her paintings. In doing so, she said that her body and her pain could also be part of her art.

That is why her painting La columna rota, from nineteen forty-four, is so powerful. In it, Frida paints herself with a broken column, split like an Ionic column, and with a steel corset holding up her torso. What in daily life was a burden becomes an image here.

The corsets are not metaphors. They are real objects, used by a real person, who turned them into a language.

In La columna rota, Frida’s body appears open, with a column that splits and nails in her skin. She wears a steel corset. It is a harsh painting. Frida appears crying, and yet she looks straight ahead. That makes the image even more powerful. There you can see that she did not want to hide her pain, but to tell it.

If you approach the display case, look for the plaster, the straps, and the brushstrokes. Notice the size. Then imagine the weight of carrying one under an embroidered blouse.

texto: Look for the painted hammer and sickle on the plaster corset
Look at the straps and the buckles: they were part of a medical device worn every day
Imagine the weight and rigidity of wearing one under an embroidered blouse

texto.Decoration: religious and communist symbols painted on the plaster

texto.pregunta: Myth: The corsets that appear in her paintings were only a metaphor for her emotional pain.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were real medical devices that Frida wore because of her spine. She herself painted several of them with her own symbols.
